title: Booking class diagram
idea: A class diagram shows the classes, their key methods and how they relate; interfaces mark the seams where one part can be swapped for another.
points: `BookingService` holds the use cases and depends on interfaces and repositories.
`ConflictPolicy` is a strategy: the overlap rule changes without touching the service.
`BookingListener` lets notification and auditing react without the service knowing them.
A dashed line with a hollow triangle means a class implements an interface.

edges.label: uses
edges.caption: The service reads rooms through `RoomRepository`, never through a raw list.

edges.label: uses
edges.caption: `BookingRepository` saves bookings and returns one room's bookings with `forRoom`.

edges.label: asks
edges.caption: Before saving, the service asks `ConflictPolicy` whether the new slot clashes.

edges.label: implements
edges.caption: `OverlapPolicy` is today's rule; a policy with buffer time could replace it.

edges.label: notifies
edges.caption: After a booking, the service calls each `BookingListener` in turn.

edges.label: implements
edges.caption: `AuditLogger` reacts by recording who booked what; the service knows neither class.

code.title: Mermaid class diagram
code.caption: The same design as Mermaid text, which lives next to the code and diffs cleanly.

walk.text: A class box lists the public methods, with types kept short.
`<<interface>>` marks a contract that has no state.
Plain arrows are associations: the service keeps each one in a field.
`<|..` is realization: the class on the right implements the interface.
Multiplicity: one room has zero or more bookings.

code.title: The ConflictPolicy contract
code.caption: One interface, one implementation, three candidate slots against one booking.

walk.text: `Booking` is a value: a record with the room, the owner and the slot.
The whole contract: a candidate, the existing bookings, a yes or no.
Same room, and each slot starts before the other ends: that is an overlap.
The caller holds the interface type, so another policy drops in unchanged.

pitfalls: Do not bury the overlap rule inside `BookingService`; put it behind `ConflictPolicy`.
Avoid drawing every getter; show roles, key methods and relations.
Name interfaces for their role, like `ConflictPolicy`, never `IConflictPolicy`.

quiz.why: `OverlapPolicy` compares room ids first. The only booking is in `R-101`, so `anyMatch` finds nothing for `R-202` and returns `false`.

takeaway: Draw the seams first: services depend on interfaces, details implement them.

starters: When should an arrow in a class diagram be composition instead of association?
Why is ConflictPolicy an interface and not a method on Room?
How much detail should a class diagram have in an interview?
